list.listitem: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction is diagnosed by a persistent overflow of tears (epiphoria) in infants aged between 3 and 12 weeks. C
Watchful waiting or lacrimal duct massage is recommended as initial therapy for the patients aged 6 to 12 months. C
If epiphora does not resolve spontaneously by 12 months, surgical procedures may be indicated. C
Dacryocystocele is an ophthalmologic emergency. C
Infectious complications should be treated promptly with systemic antibiotics. C

background.definition: Dacryostenosis (nasolacrimal duct obstruction) is blocked tear drainage to the nasal cavity causing epiphora (overflow of tears). Dacryocystocele is a swelling of the lacrimal sac caused by obstruction of both proximal and distal portions of nasolacrimal passage.

list.listitem: Up to 20% of all newborns have nasolacrimal duct obstruction.
Nasolacrimal duct obstruction is the most common cause of persistent tearing and ocular discharge in children.

Pediatric acute dacryocystitis is an uncommon complication of congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (CNLDO) and is associated with both a lower likelihood of and older age at spontaneous resolution of CNLDO symptoms.
Congenital distal valvular obstruction (most common cause).
Congenital nasolacrimal duct atresia.
Congenital abnormal valvular function.
Acquired idiopathic duct obstruction.
Acquired secondary to infection, nasal polyps/hypertrophy, radioiodine therapy, mitosis inhibitant drugs in cancer treatment, or dacryoliths.
Functional obstruction.
Delayed or incomplete embryologic canalization of lacrimal duct (which starts during the third intrauterine month and ends at birth normally) in congenital forms.
Fibrosis or mechanical obstruction in acquired forms.
Suspect duct obstruction in infants with a history of excessive and persistent tearing, ocular discharge, or swelling of the skin overlying the lacrimal sac. C
Further diagnostic testing is recommended in infants with persistent or acquired obstruction. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Swelling of the skin overlying the lacrimal sac
Erythematous tender swelling of the lacrimal sac
History of exposure to particulates, dust, etc.
Cloudy cornea, perilimbal conjunctival injection, pain
Perilimbal conjunctival injection, abnormal pupillary response
Increased intraocular pressure, perilimbal conjunctival injection, abnormal pupil response
Skin fold with rotating lashes into contact with cornea

list.listitem: Congenital tear duct obstruction presents in infants at 3 to 12 weeks of age with excessive and persistent tearing, ocular mucoid discharge, or crusting on eyelashes.
Dacryocystocele presents with bluish-gray swelling of the skin overlying the lacrimal sac just below the medial canthus.
On physical examination, there is a clear or mucoid discharge reflex from the punctum when pressure is placed over the lacrimal sac.

Fluorescein dye disappearance test: fluorescein does not clear from eye nor is it found in the nose using blue light 5 to 10 minutes after application; it is an office test to confirm or detect nonobvious cases.
Tear meniscal height measurement: accurate diagnostic indicator of obstruction and resolution after surgery.
Dacryocystography: used to locate obstruction site prior to surgery.
Lacrimal scintigraphy: more sensitive than dacryocystography in detecting proximal obstruction.
Presac reflux test is reliable for diagnosis with PPV 97% and NPV 93%.
Suspect duct obstruction in infants with a history of excessive and persistent tearing, ocular discharge, or swelling of the skin overlying the lacrimal sac.
Other infectious causes or complications must be ruled out or treated.
A fluorescein dye disappearance test may be needed to confirm the diagnosis.
Initial treatment is conservative, with watchful waiting and lacrimal massage.
Recommend expectant management with watchful waiting or lacrimal sac message in the first 6 to 12 months of life. C
Refer for probing with or without irrigation after 12 months of age. C
Consider balloon catheter dilation after 12 months of life or after failed probing. C
Use systemic antibiotics if dacryocystitis, preseptal cellulitis, or orbital cellulitis complicate obstruction occur.C
Topical antibiotics (sulfacetamide or erythromycin) are recommended for purulent discharge.

Use systemic antibiotics if dacryocystitis, preseptal cellulitis, or orbital cellulitis complicate obstruction occur. Drugs of choice would cover alpha hemolytic Streptococcus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, and Staphylococcus aureus. xcellent outcomes are reported with systemic antibiotics and early probing.

Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (CNLDO) occurs in 1 in 9 newborns. Spontaneous resolution of CNLDO occurs in 83.5% of children, and the median age at resolution is 2.4 months. The rate of resolution with probing decreased after age 15 months. Fine-wire probing of the lacrimal duct has a reported success rate of 90% in children younger than 4 years; repeated probing is successful in 56% of cases.
Nasolacrimal duct probing before 4 years of age did not require any additional intervention.
Primary probing yields the most favorable outcomes when conducted before 12 months of age, particularly under general anesthesia.
Probing combined with tobramycin/dexamethasone eye drops may be a better choice for persistant congenital nasolacrimalduct obstruction.
Silastic intubation has a reported success rate of 90% to 97%.
Normal saline or antibiotic irrigation: Hydrostatic massage has a success rate of 46% at first attempt; success rate is higher if conducted in patients up to 2 months old.

Balloon catheter dilation dacryocystoplasty with or without silicon stent placement has a reported success rate of 65% to 85% in cases of failed probing. It has a success rate of 80% as primary treatment. It is also effective in congenital obstruction and in older children who have failed previous probing. Silicon punctal plugs for acquired obstruction have a reported success rate of 84%.
External dacryocystorhinostomy has a reported success rate of 83% to 96%.
Early external dacrocystorhinostomy rather than conventional delayed external dacrocystorhinostomy (several weeks after the resolution of periocular infection) is a promising and favorable.
Endoscopic dacryocystorhinostomy is safe and can be used as alternative to External dacryocystorhinostomy with lower incidence of adverse events.

Endoscopic dacryocystorhinostomy showed similar high surgical success rate using both mono canalicular and by canalicular stents but more no canalicular stents were better tolerated and associated with fewer complications. In this retospective cohort study of 60 patients (95% using tubes) there was a 92% success rate.

Using tobramycin dexamethasone eye ointment combined with a catheter in endoscopic dacryocystorhinostomy prolongs the operation time and increases bleeding but promotes healing and improved the surgical success rate.

Endonasal laser dacryocystorhinostomy compares favorably with external dacryocystorhinostomy with a success rate of 92% to 100%. There have been high success rates reported in the treatment of recurrent obstruction after previous lacrimal surgery.
Using stent placement significantly enhanced surgical success in external approaches but lacks significant difference in internal approaches
Conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy uses a Pyrex glass tube used for upper lacrimal obstruction.
Expectant management with watchful waiting or lacrimal sac message is recommended in the first 6 months to 12 months of life. C
Hydrostatic massage consists of downward firm stroking over the bridge of the nose several times a day.
Refer patients 6- to 12-months-old to an ophthalmologist if congenital obstruction does not resolve spontaneously.
Refer to an ophthalmologist immediately if there is an acquired obstruction.
Refer to ophthalmology immediately if the diagnosis is dacryocystocele because of infection or respiratory distress caused by nasal obstruction.
Spontaneous resolution occurs by 6 months of age in up to 90% of cases. C
Symptom resolution after dacryocystorhinostomy in patient older than 80 years of age is less than younger patients.
